Distributional Regression with Tabular Foundation Models: Evaluating Probabilistic Predictions via Proper Scoring Rules

Jonas Landsgesell    Pascal Knoll
February 27, 2026
Abstract

Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs), such as TabPFN and TabICL, have revolutionized tabular deep learning by leveraging in-context learning for tabular data. These models are meant as foundation models for classification and regression settings and promise to greatly simplify deployment in practical settings because their performance is unprecedented (in terms of mean squared error or R2R^{2}, when measured on common benchmarks like TabArena or TALENT).

However, we see an important weakness of current benchmarks for the regression setting: the current benchmarks focus on evaluating win rates and performance using metrics like (root) mean squared error or R2R^{2}. Therefore, these leaderboards (implicitly and explicitly) push researchers to optimize for machine learning pipelines which elicit a good mean value estimate.

The main problem is that this approach only evaluates a point estimate (namely the mean estimator which is the Bayes estimator associated with the mean squared error loss). In this article we discuss the application of proper scoring rules for evaluating the goodness of probabilistic forecasts in distributional regression. We also propose to enhance common machine learning benchmarks with metrics for probabilistic regression. To improve the status quo and make the machine learning community aware of scoring rules for probabilistic regression, we advocate to use the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) in benchmarks for probabilistic regression. However, we also illustrate that the choice of the scoring rule changes the inductive bias of the trained model (see section 4.1). We, therefore, advocate for finetuning or promptable tabular foundation models.

   

A Preprint

Keywords Fine-tuning ⋅\cdot Benchmarking ⋅\cdot Proper Scoring Rules ⋅\cdot PFN

1 Introduction

The recent emergence of Prior-Data Fitted Networks (TabPFN) Hollmann et al. (2022); Hollmann et al. (2025) has shifted the paradigm of tabular learning from gradient boosted models to in-context learnersQu et al. (2026) which place attention on the right examples during the forward pass (without weight adaptation) of the underlying neural networks.

Besides the in-context learning, we recognize that both leading models TabPFN and also TabICLv2 perform forms of (discretized) distributional regression - an approach we greatly support since it allows for full probabilistic forecasts (in simple terms this means that the models allow to "predict a histogram over the support of potential outcomes", similar to the insets in figure 3).

Instead of creating a point estimate, TabPFN and TabICLv2 predict a discretized probability density function (approximated as a Probability Mass Function, PMF) either through an adaptive grid (TabPFNv2.5) or through estimating 999 quantiles (TabICLv2). Both approaches then need to solve the problem of guiding the model to "better" probabilistic forecasts during training. Besides architecture questions, a fundamental modeling decision is what constitutes "a good/better" probabilistic forecast. In theory, this exact question is answered through the application of a strictly proper scoring rule. A scoring rule S⁡(y→,p→^)S(\vec{y},\hat{\vec{p}}) is strictly proper if the expected score is minimized if and only if the forecast distribution matches the true distribution. However, there exist infinitely many scoring rulesGneiting and Raftery (2007). For a given decision making process with a given risk structure of a business case the optimal scoring rules need to be used. Guiding the choice of scoring rules is beyond the scope of this paper and it is itself a hard problem. We, however, want to note that it may be feasible for the practitioner to decide on a class of scoring rules which may be more appropriate than some standard scoring rules (e.g. right/left/central tendency is important). Additionally, to the above preference of using scoring rules for evaluating probabilistic forecasts, we also want to highlight, that typically different scoring rules when employed for optimum score estimationGneiting and Raftery (2007) have different inductive biasWaghmare and Ziegel (2025); Merkle and Steyvers (2013) (see section 4.1), potentially different sample efficiency in finite-sample settings11 1 Due to E^​[S⁡(y→,p→^)]≠E⁡[S⁡(y→,p→^)]\hat{E}[S(\vec{y},\hat{\vec{p}})]\neq E[S(\vec{y},\hat{\vec{p}})] and different variance of the gradient norms.

A great development of the emergence of TabPFN is that it moves away from point estimates — such as the conditional median (e.g. arising from mean absolute error minimization) or the conditional mean (from minimizing e.g. mean squared error)—to full distributional regression. Joining the previous rage against the mean, we agree that point estimates may not offer the deepest insight into a problemKneib et al. (2023) since they fail to capture aleatoric uncertainty (uncertainty you see from one-data point to another one).

We show a simple toy model to illustrate problems with the usual ordinary least squares estimation which tries to elicit a mean estimate: a regression problem where the target variable has multiple modes (see figure 3 and the appendix for the description of the data generating process and the models involved)22 2 One might argue that such a bimodal response may be due to an unobserved confounder. However, we still need to work with the data at hand and, therefore, we argue that modeling the aleatoric uncertainty is important to make better decisions..

One main takeaway from the toy model in figure 3 is that mean value estimates may fall in regions without realizations and may (depending on the utility) be completely useless (think about asking: "What could be the next outcome of a six sided die?" Even if you had a perfect mean value estimate telling you the mean value 3.5, then this would not even be a valid realization). Additionally, we also see that the usual construction of a prediction interval around the mean value estimate would cover a lot of empty space without samples (just by construction as an interval), which is inferior to estimating a conditional histogram like shown in the figure.

Interestingly, for the toy dataset, the Cross-entropy loss trained model in figure 3 differs significantly in terms of alignment with the ground truth data generating process, which indicates that at finite amount of samples:

  • •

    the convergence speed during model training may depend on the chosen loss function - even if both loss functions derive from proper scoring rules

  • •

    the sample efficiency of the complete training pipeline may depend on the loss function - even if both loss functions derive from proper scoring rules

In the table 11 in the appendix we observe that different models have different performance metrics, depending on the loss function even at otherwise identical training procedure. We also had observed this behavior on other openml datasets33 3 See https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN/pull/689 for the pull request proposing CRPS for fine-tuning TabPFN.

A proper scoring rule 𝐒:ℱ×Ω→ℝ\mathbf{S}:\mathcal{F}\times\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R} guarantees that the expected score is minimized by the true distribution Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F}:

𝔼Y∼Q​[𝐒⁡(Q,Y)]≤𝔼Y∼Q​[𝐒⁡(F,Y)]∀F∈ℱ.\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim Q}[\mathbf{S}(Q,Y)]\leq\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim Q}[\mathbf{S}(F,Y)]\quad\forall F\in\mathcal{F}. (1)

However, in practice, we minimize the sample average score E⁡[𝐒]^=1n​∑i=1n𝐒⁡(F,yi)\widehat{E[\mathbf{S}]}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{S}(F,y_{i}). While E⁡[𝐒]^\widehat{E[\mathbf{S}]} is a consistent estimator of the expectation, the optimization path at finite nn is governed by the specific gradients ∇𝐒\nabla\mathbf{S} induced by the rule.

The Logarithmic Score, 𝐒L​o​g​(F,y)=−log⁡f⁡(y)\mathbf{S}_{Log}(F,y)=-\log f(y), exhibits extreme sensitivity to the tails of Ω\Omega. Since ∇𝐒L​o​g∝1/f⁡(y)\nabla\mathbf{S}_{Log}\propto 1/f(y), the penalty for low-density observations grows toward infinity. At finite nn, even a single outlier can dominate the gradient, forcing the optimizer to prioritize tail-fitting early, often at the expense of the distribution’s central mass.

Conversely, the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) provides a more robust optimization landscape. This is best understood by expressing the CRPS as an integral over pinball losses ρτ\rho_{\tau} for all quantiles τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1]:

CRPS​(F,y)=2​∫01ρτ​(F−1​(τ),y)​𝑑τ,\text{CRPS}(F,y)=2\int_{0}^{1}\rho_{\tau}(F^{-1}(\tau),y)d\tau, (2)

where ρτ(u,y)=(y−u)(τ−𝕀{y<u})\rho_{\tau}(u,y)=(y-u)(\tau-\mathbb{I}\{y<u\}).

Because the gradient of the pinball loss is bounded (constant in magnitude), the CRPS gradient remains stable regardless of how far yy lies in the tails. Consequently, at finite nn, CRPS-based estimation focuses on the global probability mass and is less susceptible to being pulled away by sparse observations in Ω\Omega. While both rules are asymptotically equivalent in their target, their finite-sample "optimum" differs and also their behavior for tail-sensitivity (LogS) and robust mass-estimation (CRPS).

  • •

Their souls seem as dull to the charm of variety as that of the native of one of our flat English counties, whose retrospect of Switzerland was that, if its mountains could be thrown into its lakes, two nuisances would be got rid of at once." (Galton, 1889) Kneib et al. (2023)

  • •

    "Despite these well-argued perspectives, there has been little recognition that the common practice of requesting some point forecast, and then evaluating the forecasters by using some (set of) scoring function(s), is not a meaningful endeavor. In this article, we develop the perspectives of Murphy and Daan (1985) and Engelberg, Manski, and Williams (2009) and argue that effective point forecasting depends on guidance or directives, which can be given in one of two complementary ways, namely, by disclosing the scoring function ex ante to the forecaster, or by requesting a specific functional of the forecaster’s predictive distribution, such as the mean or a quantile." Gneiting (2011)

  • •

    "Although every proper scoring rule can identify the true model or the conditional distribution as its minimum in the population sense, they exhibit different inductive biases or regularization effects in finite samples. Furthermore, the computational tractability varies substantially depending on the chosen scoring rule" Waghmare and Ziegel (2025)

1.2 Contributions

We greatly appreciate the recent improvement of tabular foundation models to move away from point estimates.

However, current regression benchmarks for Tabular Machine Learning like TabArena or TALENT are still stuck in evaluating "historically important" point estimates only.

We

  • •

    propose the enhancement of regression benchmarks to account for probabilistic regression metrics derived from scoring rules, mainly CRPS by discussing a bimodal toy model.

  • •

    we provide first evaluations of realTabPFNv2.5 and TabICLv2 in terms of proper scoring rules (CRPS and beta energy score).

  • •

    we show how finetuning with different scoring rules than the one seen during pretraining in a finite-sample setting can enhance realTabPFNv2.5 performance (CRLS, beta energy score)

  • •

    we show that in theory the choice of a scoring rule can have a significant impact in terms of the inductive bias of the model (having implications for finetuning and benchmarking)Merkle and Steyvers (2013); Waghmare and Ziegel (2025)

  • •

    Additionally in the outlook, we start the discussion around a potential conflict between optimality of predictions with regard to user-supplied scoring rule and the goal to not adapt a general-purpose foundation model after pretraining.

2 Proposed Enhanced Reporting of Proper Scoring Rules in (Tabular) Regression Benchmarks

In the spirit of the seminal work by GneitingGneiting and Raftery (2007); Gneiting and Ranjan (2011); Gneiting (2011), we propose enhancing regression benchmarks for tabular foundation models by incorporating proper scoring rules. This approach shifts the focus from point-wise accuracy to a comprehensive evaluation of the predicted conditional probability distribution.

2.1 Log Score

Viewing discretized regression as a multi-class classification problem suggests the application of Cross-Entropy (CE), which corresponds to the log scoring rule which is local. This choice may be optimal if the final business objective is strictly to maximize the probability of the "correct" bin.

2.2 Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS)

However, using cross entropy loss (meaning the log scoring rule) would ignore the distance between the prediction and the ground truth (bins are not even treated as having an ordinal order like in 1<2<31<2<3 but more like completely independent concepts like "panda", "tiger", "fish"). To inject geometric awareness into the gradient, we proposed to use CRPS for finetuning TabPFN in December 202544 4 https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN/pull/689 and saw CRPS being used in TabICLv2 training in February 2026Qu et al. (2026). In a regression context, predicting y=100y=100 when the truth is y=10y=10 should be penalized more heavily than predicting y=11y=11. Still, standard Cross-Entropy treats both errors similarly if they fall into different wrong bins.

For a discretized regression output space, the discretized CRPS (equivalent to β=1\beta=1 energy score) is given by:

CRPS(F,y)≈∑i=1N(F(xi)−𝟙{xi≥y})2Δxi,CRPS(F,y)\approx\sum_{i=1}^{N}(F(x_{i})-\mathbbm{1}_{\{x_{i}\geq y\}})^{2}\Delta x_{i}, (3)

where F⁡(xi)F(x_{i}) is the predicted cumulative distribution function (e.g. obtained via cumsum of the softmax output of a neural network over the binned support). To perform optimum score estimation the expectation value (over all training samples) scoring rule needs to be taken and minimized.

However, CRPS weights all quantiles of the output space equally. This is likely, prohibitive in applications with asymmetric risk structure over the output space (see later discussion also for weighted CRPSGneiting and Ranjan (2011)).

We also think that at finite sample sizes the different scoring rules may differ (under otherwise constant conditions) in convergence speed and in sample efficiency (compare the results of the toy example in figure 3).

2.3 Continuous Ranked Logarithmic Scoring Rule (CRLS)

CRLS is defined by55 5 https://scoringrules.readthedocs.io/en/latest/theory.html

CRLS(F,y)=−∫−∞∞log|F(x)+𝟏{y≤x}−1|dx.\mathrm{CRLS}(F,y)=-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\log|F(x)+\mathbf{1}\{y\leq x\}-1|dx. (4)

2.4 Multivariate Enhancements

For y∈Ω⊆ℝdy\in\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} with d>1d>1, univariate scores are insufficient for capturing dependence. We employ and suggest to benchmark for the Energy Score (𝐒β\mathbf{S}_{\beta}) and Variogram Score (𝐒V​S,p\mathbf{S}_{VS,p}) as also done in Landsgesell (2026).

The Energy Score for β∈(0,2)\beta\in(0,2) is defined as:

𝐒β​(F,y)=𝔼F​‖X−y‖β−12​𝔼F​‖X−X′‖β\mathbf{S}_{\beta}(F,y)=\mathbb{E}_{F}\|X-y\|^{\beta}-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{F}\|X-X^{\prime}\|^{\beta} (5)

where X,X′∼FX,X^{\prime}\sim F are independent. For d=1d=1 and β=1\beta=1, 𝐒β\mathbf{S}_{\beta} reduces to the CRPS.

The Variogram Score of order p>0p>0 specifically targets the correlation structure by penalizing errors in the pairwise differences:

𝐒V​S,p​(F,y)=∑j,k=1dwj,k​(|yj−yk|p−𝔼F​|Xj−Xk|p)2\mathbf{S}_{VS,p}(F,y)=\sum_{j,k=1}^{d}w_{j,k}\left(|y_{j}-y_{k}|^{p}-\mathbb{E}_{F}|X_{j}-X_{k}|^{p}\right)^{2} (6)

where wj,kw_{j,k} are weights. While 𝐒β\mathbf{S}_{\beta} ensures strict propriety, 𝐒V​S,p\mathbf{S}_{VS,p} provides superior sensitivity to misspecified dependencies between components of yy.

3 Results

We adapt the finetuning code from github to start from the realTabPFNv2.5 checkpoint and implement custom loss functions (Beta energy score (with CRPS as special case), CRLS, and others).

We fit models on a diverse set of openML datasets for regression as shown in the various result tables. For each dataset we limit the amount of samples to randomly selected 3000 samples (random subsampling). We then perform 5 fold cross-validation on each subsampled dataset so that we can report performance on holdout data. On each split we evaluate a baseline model (always the realTabPFNv2.5) against another model (either a finetuned model or TabICLv2), so that we get paired performance metrics (per split). We report several performance metrics (M​A​EMAE, R​M​S​ERMSE, R2R^{2}, C​R​P​SCRPS, C​R​L​SCRLS, I​n​t​e​r​v​a​l​S​c​o​r​e​@​95IntervalScore@95). All metrics except R2 are better when they are lower. The improvement in R2R^{2} is reported as absolute difference in Δ​R2∗100\Delta R^{2}*100pp (to avoid statistical problems with reporting percent changes on fractions). The other improvements are reported as relative change from the baseline.

For simple interpretation we adopt the sign convention that a positive change is an improvement in the respective metric. For the metrics we first compute the change in the metric (at same split) and then compute the average afterwards.

4 Choice of Scoring Rules for Decision Making

The choice of a scoring rule matters because different scoring rules have different inductive biases Waghmare and Ziegel (2025); Merkle and Steyvers (2013). This is the reason why the scoring rule used for solving a business problem should be chosen carefully:

  • •

    Oesterheld and Conitzer (2020) describes "Decision Scoring Rules"

  • •

    Winkler et al. describe tailored scoring rules for decision making from a utility perspectiveJohnstone et al. (2011).

  • •

    The very insightful introduction example in Johnstone et al. (2011), page 2, is about making "useful" probabilistic weather forecasts for a specific use-case (an orchard) and we drew a lot of inspiration reading it - this example is very intuitive we suggest to read itJohnstone et al. (2011).

  • •

    Merkle et al.Merkle and Steyvers (2013) in their paper "Choosing a strictly proper scoring rule" describe an important effect: The "optimal forecaster" depends on the choice of a scoring rule (while all scoring rules are individually minimized by a forecast which is equal to the true distribution).

In other words, different scoring rules penalize different types of errors differently and thus the optimal forecast (the one which minimizes the expected score) can differ based on the scoring rule used. Merkle already points this out and finds that different forecasters are ranked very differently by different strictly proper scoring rules. They for example find in table 1 that the spearman correlation for the ranking of forecasters between the brier score and the log score is only 0.15. They then go on and investigate a parametrizable family of scoring rules and see how the ranking generally depends on the choice of the parameters.

For this article we follow this idea and port it to proper scoring rules which can be used in the regression setting. We choose the β\beta-energy score family and show that the optimal model depends on the choice of β\beta. To show this and for keeping the arguments as simple as possible we consider

4.1 Invesigating the effect of the choice of scoring rule on the optimal forecast

For simplicity66 6 While the following argument describes concentrated probabilistic forecasts, the argument remains untouched even if we move to not so extremely concentrated forecasts. of the argument, we consider a probabilistic forecast of the following kind:

p^i​(Y=y|X=x)=δ⁡(y−fi​(x)),\hat{p}_{i}(Y=y|X=x)=\delta(y-f_{i}(x)), (7)

where i∈{A,B,C,D,E}i\in\{A,B,C,D,E\} indexes different forecasting models (e.g. from different checkpoints of a training) and δ⁡()\delta() is the Dirac delta distribution (which collapses the probability distribution to a "pointy" probability density). In this toy model (again for simplicity of the argument) we impose the ground truth

pg​(Y=y|X=x)=δ⁡(y−g⁡(x)).p_{g}(Y=y|X=x)=\delta(y-g(x)). (8)

We choose x∈[−3,3]x\in[-3,3] (np.linspace(-3,3,1000)).

  • •

    g⁡(x)=sin⁡(x)g(x)=\sin(x)

  • •

    Model A: Small consistent bias, fA​(x)=g⁡(x)+0.1f_{A}(x)=g(x)+0.1

  • •

    Model B: Perfect with a large localized deviation, fB​(x)=g​(x)f_{B}(x)=g(x) with an additional 2.02.0 added to the middle 50 points

  • •

    Model C: Scaled version of the true function, fC​(x)=0.8⋅g⁡(x)f_{C}(x)=0.8\cdot g(x)

  • •

    Model D: Shifted version of the true function, fD​(x)=sin⁡(x+0.2)f_{D}(x)=\sin(x+0.2)

  • •

    Model E: Simple baseline at zero, fE​(x)=0f_{E}(x)=0

A typical user would now wonder which model is best? To get an intuition, we look at the models in Figure 8.

Obviously the different models make different erros which can be seen in the absolute error plot in Figure 9. Some models make small errors everywhere (model A), some models make large errors in a small region (model B), some models make medium sized errors everywhere (model C) and some models make small errors everywhere but are shifted (model D).

Now we can apply different scoring rules (from the β\beta-energy family) to see which model is optimal for which scoring rule. For a fixed choice of β\beta (one point on the x-axis in Figrue 10) the better model has the lower beta energy score.

We observe that while the model B is the best ranked model for each β≲1\beta\lesssim 1 for 1≲β1\lesssim\beta this changes and also other models switch rank at other values of β\beta, see figure 11.

Fundamentally this behavior arises from different scoring rules rating the severity of errors in Figure 9 differently (and there is even scoring rules wich penalize errors depending on the direction of the error, see for example asymmetric CRPSIacopini et al. (2023) which may be important e.g. in finance where errors have different severity depending on the direction of the error: making 100 percent more money is less severe than loosing 100 percent of money).

For simple probabilistic point masses like shown here we can even make an analytical statement: The beta energy score with β=1\beta=1 favors minimization of the mean absolute error (i.e. prefers estimating a median estimate) while for β=2\beta=2 the scoring rule prefers a minimization of mean squared error.

Derivation.

The β\beta-energy score for a forecast distribution PP and observation y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R} is defined as

ESβ​(P,y)=𝔼X∼P​[|X−y|β]−12​𝔼X,X′∼P​[|X−X′|β],0<β≤2,\mathrm{ES}_{\beta}(P,\,y)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}\bigl[|X-y|^{\beta}\bigr]-\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{X,\,X^{\prime}\sim P}\bigl[|X-X^{\prime}|^{\beta}\bigr],\qquad 0<\beta\leq 2, (9)

where XX and X′X^{\prime} are independent draws from PP.

Now suppose the forecast is a probabilistic point mass, i.e. P=δm^P=\delta_{\hat{m}} for some point estimate m^∈ℝ\hat{m}\in\mathbb{R}. Both XX and X′X^{\prime} equal m^\hat{m} almost surely, so the second term in (9) vanishes and the score reduces to

ESβ​(δm^,y)=|m^−y|β.\mathrm{ES}_{\beta}(\delta_{\hat{m}},\,y)=|\hat{m}-y|^{\beta}. (10)

The optimal point estimate m^∗\hat{m}^{*} minimises the expected score over observations y∼Qy\sim Q for some true data distribution QQ:

m^∗=arg​minm^⁡𝔼y∼Q​[|m^−y|β].\hat{m}^{*}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\hat{m}}\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}\!\left[|\hat{m}-y|^{\beta}\right]. (11)

Case β=1\beta=1.  Equation (11) becomes minm^⁡𝔼⁡[|m^−y|]\min_{\hat{m}}\,\mathbb{E}[|\hat{m}-y|], i.e. minimisation of the mean absolute error (MAE). The unique minimiser is the median of QQ, since

∂∂m^​𝔼​[|m^−y|]=Pr⁡(y<m^)−Pr⁡(y>m^)=0⟺m^=median⁡(Q).\frac{\partial}{\partial\hat{m}}\,\mathbb{E}[|\hat{m}-y|]=\Pr(y<\hat{m})-\Pr(y>\hat{m})=0\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\hat{m}=\mathrm{median}(Q). (12)

Case β=2\beta=2.  Equation (11) becomes minm^⁡𝔼⁡[(m^−y)2]\min_{\hat{m}}\,\mathbb{E}[(\hat{m}-y)^{2}], i.e. minimisation of the mean squared error (MSE). Setting the derivative to zero gives

∂∂m^​𝔼​[(m^−y)2]=2​(m^−𝔼⁡[y])=0⟺m^∗=𝔼⁡[y]=mean⁡(Q).\frac{\partial}{\partial\hat{m}}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[(\hat{m}-y)^{2}\right]=2\,(\hat{m}-\mathbb{E}[y])=0\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\hat{m}^{*}=\mathbb{E}[y]=\mathrm{mean}(Q). (13)

Hence the β\beta-energy score with β=2\beta=2 is minimised by reporting the mean of the predictive distribution.

The choice of the scoring rule determines how different types of errors are penalized and thus the optimal forecast (the one which minimizes the expected score) can differ based on the scoring rule used. This is true, despite every scoring rule being strictly proper (i.e. every scoring rule is minimized by the true distribution). The reason is that different scoring rules penalize different types of errors differently and thus the optimal forecast (the one which minimizes the expected score) can differ based on the scoring rule used.

We leave it as an open question how to best choose a scoring rule for general purpose tabular foundation model pretraining and how to enable adaptation to arbitrary business case with high severity for certain errors (like in finance or pharmaceutical production). We describe some possible routes to explore in the outlook section 7.

5 Discussion

Across the datasets evaluated, finetuning with beta-energy score (β=1.8\beta=1.8) and CRLS both tend to improve realTabPFNv2.5 on the majority of metrics and datasets (as indicated by the W/L/T counts in Tables 2 and 4). However, improvements are modest in median terms (typically <2%<2\%) and vary considerably across datasets.

The aggregate results further suggest that TabICLv2 may be a stronger probabilistic model than realTabPFNv2.5 in terms of CRPS, CRLS, and Interval Score, with TabICLv2 winning on the majority of evaluated datasets (Tables 6, 8). The margin varies substantially across datasets (e.g. large gains on Mercedes Benz and Pol, but losses on Puma8NH and House Sales).

Additional experiments examining how finetuning performance scales with dataset size would be valuable to better understand whether the observed differences are robust across data regimes.

We illustrate in section 4.1 that the choice of scoring rule can change the ranking of forecasting models — at least in the considered toy setting of Dirac-delta forecasts over a smooth ground truth function. Under this simplification, the result follows analytically from the β\beta-energy score reducing to an LβL^{\beta} norm. Whether this ranking sensitivity carries over to actual trained distributional models in realistic tabular settings remains an open empirical question. That said, the theoretical argument and the empirical literature Waghmare and Ziegel (2025); Merkle and Steyvers (2013) both support the view that the choice of scoring rule for pretraining or finetuning a tabular foundation model is non-trivial and may affect which use-cases the model is best suited for Oesterheld and Conitzer (2020); Johnstone et al. (2011).

6 Limitations: Rare or Extreme Events

We want to highlight that optimal scoring rule estimation (minimizing/maximizing the expected value of a scoring rule) is inherently not well suited for eliciting properties which are only realized in rare events (fall in the area where no data was observed or in 1D are in the tail of a distribution). This was well argued in recent years for the case of one dimensional distributions but equally carries over to higher dimensions. Lerch et al. (2017); Brehmer and Strokorb (2019) Inherently, this problem is related to epistemic uncertainty (uncertainty due to not having training data). Based on this insight also PFNs (trained to optimize mean scoring rules) should be applied with care if risk associated mainly with rare (tail) events or events outside the support of the examples in the supplied context.

7 Outlook

While we discussed how to properly measure the goodness of a probabilistic forecast - namely by applying proper scoring rules, we highlight, that this discussion is not finished. Gneiting pointed out in Gneiting and Ranjan (2011) that situations with asymmetric risk (finance, weather forecasting etc.) may require to optimize for specific point estimates (via scoring functions suitable to elicit a specific point estimate). In such a case, we wonder how tabular foundation models would adapt to specific user supplied scoring functions (so that optimality is guaranteed). We point out a conflict of

  • •

    a foundation model which is not altered by a user at all after pretraining is finished

  • •

    the need to take into account that the optimal scoring function depends on the use-case at hand (must be supplied by the user since the user intention dictates the utility).

We see that Fine-Tuning of foundation models could be one route to enable optimal predictions for arbitrary scoring functions. Another route could be to enable task-token conditional probability prediction in case of asymmetric risk structures (a user would prompt the model with a desired scoring rule which should be optimal, but this behaviour would need to be pretrained). Such a task-token conditional probability prediction could output probability estimates which are optimal under some parametrizable family of scoring rules (like e.g. the beta energy score family). However there is infinitely many scoring rules and different families of scoring rules so that it is unlcear if pre-training with taks-tokens can in general adapt to arbitrary scoring rules as objectives. Potentially, tabular foundation models for high stakes applications need to make sensible choices for task conditioning for certain applications (finance, pharma production, etc.).

7.1 Example: Weighted CRPS (wCRPS)

Accounting for asymmetric risk structures, a modeler can choose to apply the different versions of weighted CRPSGneiting and Ranjan (2011) - a family of strictly proper scoring rules which enables e.g. emphasizing prediction quality for the left/right tail of a distribution which makes sense when dealing with e.g. energy forecasting or forecasting weather events with asymmetric cost.

Lw​C​R​P​S≈∑i=1Nw(xi)(F(xi)−𝟙{xi≥y})2Δxi,L_{wCRPS}\approx\sum_{i=1}^{N}w(x_{i})(F(x_{i})-\mathbbm{1}_{\{x_{i}\geq y\}})^{2}\Delta x_{i}, (14)

7.2 Example: Interval Score

The Interval ScoreGneiting and Raftery (2007) targets the (1−α)(1-\alpha) central interval and is strictly proper, directly answering "how well is the interval estimated?" for a given significance level α\alpha:

Sα(F,y)=(u−l)+2α(l−y)𝕀{y<l}+2α(y−u)𝕀{y>u}S_{\alpha}(F,y)=(u-l)+\frac{2}{\alpha}(l-y)\mathbb{I}\{y<l\}+\frac{2}{\alpha}(y-u)\mathbb{I}\{y>u\} (15)

where [l,u][l,u] are the α/2\alpha/2 and 1−α/21-\alpha/2 quantiles of the prediction FF.

This specific scoring rule highlights that different scoring rules favor optimization in distinct regions of the probability mass function (PMF); in the extreme case of the interval score, the two boundary quantiles are of primary importance. Because we hypothesize that each scoring rule aligns with a specific utility, general-purpose models may fail to achieve optimality for specialized downstream tasks where the cost of error is non-uniform across the domain Ω\Omega.

9 Appendix

9.1 Toy-Models to investigate finite sample effects

9.1.1 Data Generating Process

We simulate a dataset where the target variable yy exhibits a bimodal conditional distribution given a feature xx. This is achieved by generating yy values from two distinct linear relationships:

y1=m1​x+c1+ϵ1y_{1}=m_{1}x+c_{1}+\epsilon_{1} (16)
y2=m2​x+c2+ϵ2y_{2}=m_{2}x+c_{2}+\epsilon_{2} (17)

where ϵ1,ϵ2∼N⁡(0,σ2)\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}) represent independent Gaussian noise. For each observation of xx, the corresponding yy is randomly sampled from either y1y_{1} or y2y_{2}, creating a bimodal output distribution P⁡(y|x)P(y|x).

9.1.2 Toy Models

To evaluate the efficacy of probabilistic forecasting in such a scenario, we compare several modeling strategies:

Baseline Regression Models

  • •

    Least Squares (LS): A Random Forest Regressor trained with a squared error criterion, approximating the conditional mean: E⁡[y|x]E[y|x].

  • •

    Least Absolute Deviations (LAD): A Random Forest Regressor trained with an absolute error criterion, approximating the conditional median: Median​(y|x)\text{Median}(y|x).

Probabilistic Classification Models These models predict probabilities across N=50N=50 discrete bins of the yy-variable. The neural networks are optimized using the Adam optimizer and are simple multi-layer perceptron (MLP) featuring an input layer, two hidden layers with 64 neurons each using tanh\tanh activations, and a Softmax output layer for nn bins.

  • •

    PyTorch Cross-Entropy (CE) Model: A feed-forward neural network trained with Cross-Entropy loss (log score), aiming to maximize the probability of the true bin.

  • •

    PyTorch Ranked Probability Score (RPS) Model: A neural network trained directly to minimize the expected CRPS, which optimizes the accuracy of the cumulative distribution function (CDF).

  • •

    XGBoost RPS Model: An XGBoost vectorleaf classifier utilizing a custom objective function that directly optimizes the Continuous Ranked Probability Score

    ⬇
    1 import numpy as np
    2 import torch
    3 import torch.nn.functional as F
    4
    5 def crps_objective(preds, dtrain):
    6 """
    7 Improved RPS Objective for XGBoost.
    8 Optimized for multi-class flattening and numerical stability.
    9 """
    10 # 1. Labels
    11 labels = dtrain.get_label().astype(int)
    12
    13 # 2. Reshape preds if multi-class (XGBoost passes them flat)
    14 num_samples = labels.shape[0]
    15 num_bins = preds.size // num_samples
    16 preds = preds.reshape(num_samples, num_bins)
    17
    18 # 3. Softmax for Probabilities (using Torch for speed/consistency)
    19 preds_tensor = torch.tensor(preds, dtype=torch.float32)
    20 probs = F.softmax(preds_tensor, dim=1).numpy()
    21
    22 # 4. One-Hot Targets
    23 target_one_hot = np.zeros_like(probs)
    24 target_one_hot[np.arange(num_samples), labels] = 1
    25
    26 # 5. CDFs
    27 pred_cdf = np.cumsum(probs, axis=1)
    28 target_cdf = np.cumsum(target_one_hot, axis=1)
    29 cdf_diff = pred_cdf - target_cdf # (B, K)
    30
    31 # 6. Gradient Calculation
    32 # dRPS/dp_j = 2 * sum_{k=j}^{K} (pred_cdf_k - target_cdf_k)
    33 grad_p = 2 * np.flip(np.cumsum(np.flip(cdf_diff, axis=1), axis=1), axis=1)
    34
    35 # Convert grad w.r.t probability to grad w.r.t logit (z_j)
    36 # grad_z_j = prob_j * (grad_p_j - sum_i(grad_p_i * prob_i))
    37 weighted_grad_p = np.sum(grad_p * probs, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    38 grad_z = probs * (grad_p - weighted_grad_p)
    39
    40 # 7. Hessian Calculation
    41 # Robust approximation: 2 * prob * (1 - prob)
    42 hess_z = 2.0 * probs * (1.0 - probs)
    43
    44 return grad_z.flatten(), hess_z.flatten()
    45
    46 def rps_metric(preds, dtrain):
    47 """Evaluation metric for RPS."""
    48 labels = dtrain.get_label().astype(int)
    49 num_samples = labels.shape[0]
    50 num_bins = preds.size // num_samples
    51
    52 preds = preds.reshape(num_samples, num_bins)
    53 probs = F.softmax(torch.tensor(preds), dim=1).numpy()
    54
    55 target_one_hot = np.zeros_like(probs)
    56 target_one_hot[np.arange(num_samples), labels] = 1
    57
    58 pred_cdf = np.cumsum(probs, axis=1)
    59 target_cdf = np.cumsum(target_one_hot, axis=1)
    60
    61 rps = np.mean(np.sum((pred_cdf - target_cdf)**2, axis=1))
    62 return ’RPS’, rps

9.1.3 Model Performance Comparison

The performance is evaluated using Mean Squared Error (MSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the Ranked Probability Score (CRPS).

9.1.4 Summary

In this bimodal dataset scenario:

  • •

    Regression Failure: Least Squares and Least Absolute Deviations models struggle to capture the underlying distribution, as point estimates often fall in the low-probability "valley" between modes.

  • •

    RPS Advantage: Both the PyTorch and XGBoost models trained with the custom CRPS objective provide superior probabilistic forecasts.

  • •

    Conclusion: While MSE and MAE (as specific scoring functions, see Gneiting and Ranjan (2011)) provide insights into point prediction, CRPS is the appropriate metric for evaluating complex conditional distributions. The XGBoost model with the custom CRPS objective demonstrated the most robust performance.
